extraction.body: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. extraction.body: SpaceX Starmind won FCC approval for up to 1 million AI data center satellites on November 25, 2026. You get the first US license for space-based data centers, but the FCC set aside heat and astronomy objections and still hasn't ruled on disposal above 600 km. The FCC gave SpaceX permission on November 25 to launch up to 1 million Starmind satellites, the first time the US has approved a constellation of data centers in space. That sounds like a green light for Elon Musk’s plan to move AI computing into orbit, and in one sense it is. But when I read the FCC’s order, I found it rules on far less than the headline suggests, because the agency set aside the biggest objections as outside its authority and postponed a decision that four of Starmind’s six orbital layers depend on. So what is Starmind, why would anyone build a data center in space, and what’s still undecided? SpaceX Starmind is a planned network of satellites that run AI computing chips in orbit and send the results back to Earth over laser links to Starlink, SpaceX’s internet satellites. Each satellite, called AI1, has a 75-meter wingspan of solar panels and a compute payload rated at up to 250 kilowatts at peak and 175 kilowatts on average, according to SpaceX’s Starmind page . SpaceX is designing that payload with Nvidia, as we covered when SpaceX and Nvidia announced the AI1 partnership , and says its Texas Gigasat Factory could start building the satellites as soon as late 2027. The scale is hard to picture, so I did the math. At 175 kilowatts each, a full constellation of 1 million satellites would draw about 175 gigawatts on average, roughly the output of 175 large nuclear reactors. For comparison, about 17,000 satellites are in orbit today, by Broadband Breakfast’s count. AI data centers on Earth are running into two limits, which are finding enough electricity and getting rid of heat. SpaceX argues that space solves both, since satellites in a sun-synchronous orbit (an orbit that keeps them in near-constant sunlight) get solar power without weather or grid connections, and heat can radiate into space without the chillers and cooling towers ground data centers need. The catch is that radiating heat in a vacuum takes very large radiators, and several people who commented to the FCC questioned whether orbital data centers can manage heat at all. SpaceX isn’t alone in betting they can. Blue Origin has asked the FCC for up to 51,600 satellites under its Project Sunrise, and Google is testing chips in orbit for its own Project Suncatcher, which we compared with SpaceX’s plan in our look at Google’s Project Suncatcher . The FCC says it’s still reviewing other orbital data center proposals. Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society all asked the FCC to deny the application, and Amazon called it “incomplete, speculative, and unrealistic” in its petition. The FCC’s answer, in its Memorandum Opinion and Order , is narrower than a ruling on the merits. The radio license itself covers Starmind’s backup and emergency links, since its main laser links fall outside the FCC’s jurisdiction. That framing shaped everything else. The astronomers argued that waste heat from a million satellites could raise the infrared glow of the sky and harm research, and the FCC replied that such “non-spectrum related impacts” are outside the scope of its review. Doubts about whether the technology works, or how it handles heat, got the same answer. For visible-light astronomy, the FCC relied on SpaceX’s commitment to coordinate with the National Science Foundation rather than adding conditions. In other words, these concerns weren’t resolved, they just weren’t the FCC’s to decide. My read is that the FCC’s pending ruling on satellite disposal matters more to Starmind’s real size than the 1 million figure does. SpaceX asked to send retired satellites above 600 km into far-away disposal orbits rather than burning them up in the atmosphere, and the FCC deferred that request. Four of Starmind’s six orbital layers sit above 600 km, so until that ruling comes, the most clearly usable space is the two lowest layers, including the sun-synchronous one between 565 and 585 km that suits a solar-powered satellite best. I’d expect SpaceX’s first Starmind satellites to go there. If the FCC approves the disposal plan, the limit shifts from regulators to launch costs and chip supply, which is where SpaceX’s Starship rocket and its Terafab chip factory plan come in. Starmind is SpaceX’s planned constellation of up to 1 million solar-powered satellites that run AI computing in orbit and send results to Earth through Starlink’s laser network. Each AI1 satellite carries a compute payload of up to 250 kilowatts at peak. The FCC requires SpaceX to have its first Starmind satellite operating by November 25, 2033, half the constellation by 2038 and all of it by 2040. SpaceX says manufacturing could start as soon as late 2027. Not yet. Starmind is the first orbital data center constellation the FCC has approved, and the agency says it’s still reviewing other proposals, including plans from Blue Origin and startups. Blue Origin has asked the FCC for up to 51,600 satellites under its Project Sunrise, and Google is testing chips in orbit for its own Project Suncatcher, which we compared with SpaceX’s plan in our look at Google’s Project Suncatcher . The FCC says it’s still reviewing other orbital data center proposals.

Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society all asked the FCC to deny the application, and Amazon called it “incomplete, speculative, and unrealistic” in its petition. The FCC’s answer, in its Memorandum Opinion and Order , is narrower than a ruling on the merits. The radio license itself covers Starmind’s backup and emergency links, since its main laser links fall outside the FCC’s jurisdiction.

That framing shaped everything else. The astronomers argued that waste heat from a million satellites could raise the infrared glow of the sky and harm research, and the FCC replied that such “non-spectrum related impacts” are outside the scope of its review. Doubts about whether the technology works, or how it handles heat, got the same answer. For visible-light astronomy, the FCC relied on SpaceX’s commitment to coordinate with the National Science Foundation rather than adding conditions. In other words, these concerns weren’t resolved, they just weren’t the FCC’s to decide.

My read is that the FCC’s pending ruling on satellite disposal matters more to Starmind’s real size than the 1 million figure does. SpaceX asked to send retired satellites above 600 km into far-away disposal orbits rather than burning them up in the atmosphere, and the FCC deferred that request. Four of Starmind’s six orbital layers sit above 600 km, so until that ruling comes, the most clearly usable space is the two lowest layers, including the sun-synchronous one between 565 and 585 km that suits a solar-powered satellite best. I’d expect SpaceX’s first Starmind satellites to go there. If the FCC approves the disposal plan, the limit shifts from regulators to launch costs and chip supply, which is where SpaceX’s Starship rocket and its Terafab chip factory plan come in.

Starmind is SpaceX’s planned constellation of up to 1 million solar-powered satellites that run AI computing in orbit and send results to Earth through Starlink’s laser network. Each AI1 satellite carries a compute payload of up to 250 kilowatts at peak.

The FCC requires SpaceX to have its first Starmind satellite operating by November 25, 2033, half the constellation by 2038 and all of it by 2040. SpaceX says manufacturing could start as soon as late 2027.
Not yet. Starmind is the first orbital data center constellation the FCC has approved, and the agency says it’s still reviewing other proposals, including plans from Blue Origin and startups.

sources.title: U.S. approves SpaceX plan to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space - CBC
passages: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is authorizing Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy a constellation of one million satellites for data centres in space, the agency said on Wednesday.
Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility.
SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system.
The growing network currently ​has more than 11,000 satellites in space.
Amazon's rival satellite unit Leo and ⁠others have criticized the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites ⁠and ⁠that it could take centuries ​to do so.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March.
The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet ​rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

"By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and ⁠energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centres," SpaceX told the FCC.
Here's how that could impact the atmosphere and the night sky
SpaceX's request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company's ⁠next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites.

"Amazon should focus on ​getting Amazon's house in ⁠order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," Carr said.
SpaceX's Starship successfully returns to launch tower for first time

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Analyst Michaël van de Poppe says there can be a two-stage Bitcoin bounce. He said the process will start with a rapid relief rally, then a steeper rise after the Nasdaq bottoms out. Bitcoin is trading under its 200-day moving average, which is a measure of the digital currency's average price over the past 200 days. Bitcoin (BTC) could jump back to $100,000 in the first quarter of 2027, analyst Michaël van de Poppe said, attributing its drop toward a two-year low to Nasdaq selling rather than any crypto-specific problems. The selloff has been an "extreme outlier," Van de Poppe, founder of MN Capital, said during a Thursday appearance on Bitcoin Magazine's BMTV. He foresaw a two-stage Bitcoin bounce, starting with a rapid relief rally, then a steeper rise after the Nasdaq bottoms out. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox The Bitcoin drop is not very much related to the crypto industry, said Van de Poppe. He said it is being sold by institutional investors to hedge risk in other holdings, and in a panic, everything falls together. Gold, silver, AI stocks, and Bitcoin are all down in the latest rout. Van de Poppe said that Bitcoin behaves like stocks when the markets change. "It still trades like a risk-on asset," he said. He added that Bitcoin trails when stocks bounce back, since asset managers require more confidence before buying it back. He thinks it will take a few days of the Nasdaq being up before money flows back into Bitcoin ETFs. "The recent drop was the kind of move you get about once a year," he said. Such moves tend to trigger a 15% to 40% short-term rally, which would put Bitcoin at $68,000 to $72,000, he said. Van de Poppe also said that the bull markets of 2024 and 2025 only happened because money poured into ETFs. "If not for this, Bitcoin would probably stay in a bear market for four to five years, trading around $20,000 to $30,000," he said. That flow has now reversed. Spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $5.7 billion in November through Friday, beating the previous record of $4.51 billion set in June, SoSoValue data showed. The analyst said, "A lasting recovery will take longer." Bitcoin is trading under its 200-day moving average, which is a measure of the digital currency's average price over the past 200 days. It needs to get back to that level and to its 21-week average, which has typically taken four to eight weeks, he said. The setup, he said, was reminiscent of late 2015, when a similar shakeout led to a sharp rally. He also expects the next bull market to match 2017 rather than deliver smaller gains. Stablecoins, tokenization, and AI agents finally give crypto real use outside its own industry, he said, comparing the moment to the early days of Apple's (AAPL) iPhone. Van de Poppe dismissed concerns that AI or quantum computing could break Bitcoin. The network has already survived a lot, he said. "If the agentic era or quantum can break Bitcoin, I think we have way bigger problems to deal with," he said. He has been calling for a rebound for weeks. Earlier this month, he said Bitcoin could recover after Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, as it did after SpaceX's (SPCX) listing in June. Bitcoin's price was down over 3% during the past 24 hours. Bitcoin (BTC) could jump back to $100,000 in the first quarter of 2027, analyst Michaël van de Poppe said, attributing its drop toward a two-year low to Nasdaq selling rather than any crypto-specific problems.

The selloff has been an "extreme outlier," Van de Poppe, founder of MN Capital, said during a Thursday appearance on Bitcoin Magazine's BMTV. He foresaw a two-stage Bitcoin bounce, starting with a rapid relief rally, then a steeper rise after the Nasdaq bottoms out.

The Bitcoin drop is not very much related to the crypto industry, said Van de Poppe. He said it is being sold by institutional investors to hedge risk in other holdings, and in a panic, everything falls together. Gold, silver, AI stocks, and Bitcoin are all down in the latest rout.

Van de Poppe said that Bitcoin behaves like stocks when the markets change. "It still trades like a risk-on asset," he said. He added that Bitcoin trails when stocks bounce back, since asset managers require more confidence before buying it back. He thinks it will take a few days of the Nasdaq being up before money flows back into Bitcoin ETFs.
"The recent drop was the kind of move you get about once a year," he said. Such moves tend to trigger a 15% to 40% short-term rally, which would put Bitcoin at $68,000 to $72,000, he said.

Van de Poppe also said that the bull markets of 2024 and 2025 only happened because money poured into ETFs. "If not for this, Bitcoin would probably stay in a bear market for four to five years, trading around $20,000 to $30,000," he said.
That flow has now reversed. Spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $5.7 billion in November through Friday, beating the previous record of $4.51 billion set in June, SoSoValue data showed.

The analyst said, "A lasting recovery will take longer." Bitcoin is trading under its 200-day moving average, which is a measure of the digital currency's average price over the past 200 days. It needs to get back to that level and to its 21-week average, which has typically taken four to eight weeks, he said. The setup, he said, was reminiscent of late 2015, when a similar shakeout led to a sharp rally.

He also expects the next bull market to match 2017 rather than deliver smaller gains. Stablecoins, tokenization, and AI agents finally give crypto real use outside its own industry, he said, comparing the moment to the early days of Apple's (AAPL) iPhone.

Van de Poppe dismissed concerns that AI or quantum computing could break Bitcoin. The network has already survived a lot, he said. "If the agentic era or quantum can break Bitcoin, I think we have way bigger problems to deal with," he said.
He has been calling for a rebound for weeks. Earlier this month, he said Bitcoin could recover after Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, as it did after SpaceX's (SPCX) listing in June.

Bitcoin's price was down over 3% during the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BTC moved to 'bullish' from 'neutral' zone, while chatter around it shifted to 'normal' from 'high' over the past day.

The analyst also made a case that crypto now has uses beyond its own borders, pointing to stablecoins, tokenization and AI agents and likening the moment to the early days of Apple's (AAPL) iPhone.
He brushed aside fears that artificial intelligence or quantum computing could compromise the network, which he said has already survived far worse.

In a separate monthly roadmap posted on X, he laid out a path in which Bitcoin pushes higher into the end of November and settles between $64,000 and $65,000, then tests the $70,000 to $72,000 zone in December.

Speaking Thursday on Bitcoin Magazine's BMTV, the analyst described the recent decline as an "extreme outlier" and argued that institutional investors are dumping the asset to hedge risk elsewhere.
Gold, silver, artificial intelligence stocks and Bitcoin all fell together in the latest rout, he noted, adding that "it still trades like a risk-on asset."

Notably, in the years when the quarter ended positively, the gains often exceeded 45%, suggesting that the forecasts align with Bitcoin’s typical performance during this time. While the average return for the fourth quarter stands at around 77%, it has been significantly influenced by extreme gains in years like 2013 and 2017. The median return, which offers a more stable figure, is about 48%, slightly above what the current predictions require. However, recent years show a weaker trend: Bitcoin gained only 5% in the fourth quarter of 2021, lost 15% in 2022, and dropped 23% in 2025, making it the second-worst fourth quarter on record after 2018. Bitcoin was much smaller as an asset in 2013, which allowed for sharper price movements. While both predictions are historically possible, the timeline for achieving them looks challenging. Additionally, the correction van de Poppe allowed in October could undermine hopes for an immediate recovery by January. If Bitcoin does not reach $125,000 by December 31, Bernstein’s year-end call will not materialize, though their mid-2027 target of $150,000 remains. extraction.body: In a bold forecast, Bernstein predicts that Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) could hit $125,000 by December 31, 2026. To reach this target, Bitcoin needs to climb around 45%. Meanwhile, Michaël van de Poppe anticipates a potential new all-time high in January 2027, requiring a rise of about 46%. These predictions are among the most optimistic Bitcoin price predictions for the final quarter of the year. As of October 5, Bitcoin is trading at $86,093, up 8% over the last month but down 30% over the past year. This price is also 32% below its record of $126,080, set in October 2025. So, has Bitcoin ever made such a substantial leap in the fourth quarter, and does its history support these predictions? Analysts at Bernstein, led by Gautam Chhugani, set the $125,000 target in a research note released in late August and also suggested a mid-2027 target of $150,000. Their predictions are based on three main factors: Michaël van de Poppe, the founder of MN Fund, offers a different outlook. In forecasts released on September 1, he expects Bitcoin to rise to at least $82,700, possibly reaching $90,000, before trading sideways for two to four months. This timeline suggests that new all-time highs may occur between November and January 2027. Van de Poppe also said a typical bull market might see a 20% to 40% correction after reaching a recent peak, predicting such a decline could happen in September or October. Bitcoin briefly surged to $87,397 on September 21 , surpassing his initial target, but the October timeframe is still uncertain. If Bitcoin dropped 20% from $86,093, it would fall to about $68,900, requiring an 83% climb to hit the record. A 40% fall would lower it to roughly $51,700, necessitating a 144% increase to set a new high. Data from CoinGlass reveals how Bitcoin’s performance in the fourth quarter has varied over the years: In seven of the past 13 years, Bitcoin has gained 45% or more in the fourth quarter. However, it has also lost value in five years. Notably, in the years when the quarter ended positively, the gains often exceeded 45%, suggesting that the forecasts align with Bitcoin’s typical performance during this time. While the average return for the fourth quarter stands at around 77%, it has been significantly influenced by extreme gains in years like 2013 and 2017. The median return, which offers a more stable figure, is about 48%, slightly above what the current predictions require. However, recent years show a weaker trend: Bitcoin gained only 5% in the fourth quarter of 2021, lost 15% in 2022, and dropped 23% in 2025, making it the second-worst fourth quarter on record after 2018. Bitcoin was much smaller as an asset in 2013, which allowed for sharper price movements. While both predictions are historically possible, the timeline for achieving them looks challenging. Bitcoin needs a fourth quarter as strong as its median gain while grappling with a 30% decline over the year and just a few months remaining. Additionally, the correction van de Poppe allowed in October could undermine hopes for an immediate recovery by January. If Bitcoin does not reach $125,000 by December 31, Bernstein’s year-end call will not materialize, though their mid-2027 target of $150,000 remains. Similarly, if Bitcoin doesn’t surpass $126,080 by the end of January 2027, van de Poppe’s timeframe for a new high will have closed as well. Black Friday deals are more confusing than ever these days. Most retailers spend November teasing limited-time offers, but the reality is that the deepest discounts typically arrive a lot earlier than you'd expect. Having tracked gaming sales for years, one thing is clear: once a deal hits from an official gaming sale like this one, it usually sticks for the rest of the month at least. That means the prices you see now on games and accessories are very likely the ones that’ll hold through to December. If you’ve been holding out for a solid deal, there’s no need to wait any longer. These offers are reliable, worthwhile, and unlikely to get any better. In fact, some deals are so good, they could even sell out before you get the chance to buy them if you decide to wait around anymore. My advice? Grab the games and hardware you’ve had your eye on, there’s no risk of Black Friday regret. Trust me on this! Want more gaming deals? I've left the rest of the best PS5 deals in the Black Friday sale just below, but you should also keep an eye out for the rest of our coverage over the next few weeks. I'll admit I'm a little biased here, but I really do think there's still plenty of life left in physical games - even if Sony doesn't. Sony is planning to stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation releases from January 2028, meaning disc-based games are on the chopping block. While existing physical releases won't suddenly disappear, the prospect of future PlayStation games becoming digital-only is a worrying one for anyone who enjoys building a collection or wants to be able to play their games when the servers inevitably shut down one day. Sony has attributed the decision to changing consumer preferences, so if we want physical games to stick around, we need to make our voices heard where it matters most: our wallets. Buying physical gives you options that digital downloads simply don't. You can lend games to friends, trade them in, sell them when you're finished, or keep building a collection that you can actually see and hold. Physical retailers also compete with one another on pricing, meaning you're not entirely at the mercy of the PlayStation Store when hunting for a bargain. There's a wider ecosystem worth supporting, too, from independent game shops and second-hand retailers to collectors and gaming preservationists. An increasingly digital-only future means fewer choices over where we buy our games, how much we pay, and what we can do with them afterwards. So, if you've been sitting on the fence about picking up a physical copy of a game you've been eyeing, perhaps now's the time. Keep building that collection, support the retailers still selling physical games, and show Sony there's still an audience for discs. Buying a few games won't single-handedly reverse its decision, but if we stop buying them altogether, we're hardly going to convince anyone to keep making them. extraction.body: Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. Whether you're preparing for holiday travel, looking for a reliable pair of headphones for work, or shopping for a gift for a music lover, there's plenty to like about these headphones. Sony has built a reputation for making excellent noise-canceling headphones, and the WH-1000XM4C draws on the technology behind its premium 1000X series. The headphones help reduce distractions like airplane engine noise, busy office chatter, and traffic sounds. This makes it easier to enjoy your favorite podcasts, focus on work, or relax with some music during your daily commute. The headphones also use AI-powered technology to help restore some of the audio detail lost when music files are compressed, resulting in a richer listening experience. They support high-resolution wireless audio with compatible devices. And if you prefer punchier bass or brighter vocals, you can fine-tune the sound to your liking through the Sony Sound Connect app. Weighing approximately nine ounces, the WH-1000XM4C is lightweight enough for extended listening sessions. Its foldable design and included carrying case also make it easy to pack into a backpack or carry-on without taking up too much space. Multiple microphones help your voice come through clearly during calls, while touch controls on the earcup let you adjust the volume, skip songs, and pause playback without reaching for your phone. Considering that the Sony WH-1000XM4C launched in September, getting them for 34% off is a particularly attractive Black Friday deal . extraction.body: Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up. These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027.

Launched in September at $300, the noise-canceling headphones are now available for just $198. These headphones combine premium sound quality, effective noise cancellation, and long battery life in a lightweight, foldable design. Whether you're preparing for holiday travel, looking for a reliable pair of headphones for work, or shopping for a gift for a music lover, there's plenty to like about these headphones. Sony has built a reputation for making excellent noise-canceling headphones, and the WH-1000XM4C draws on the technology behind its premium 1000X series. The headphones help reduce distractions like airplane engine noise, busy office chatter, and traffic sounds. This makes it easier to enjoy your favorite podcasts, focus on work, or relax with some music during your daily commute. The headphones also use AI-powered technology to help restore some of the audio detail lost when music files are compressed, resulting in a richer listening experience. They support high-resolution wireless audio with compatible devices. And if you prefer punchier bass or brighter vocals, you can fine-tune the sound to your liking through the Sony Sound Connect app. Weighing approximately nine ounces, the WH-1000XM4C is lightweight enough for extended listening sessions. Its foldable design and included carrying case also make it easy to pack into a backpack or carry-on without taking up too much space. Battery life shouldn't be much of a concern either, as the headphones offer up to 27 hours of listening time on a single charge. And if you forget to charge them before heading out, a quick three-minute charge provides up to an hour of playback. The headphones can also connect to two Bluetooth devices at once, so you can switch between your laptop and smartphone without constantly disconnecting and reconnecting. Multiple microphones help your voice come through clearly during calls, while touch controls on the earcup let you adjust the volume, skip songs, and pause playback without reaching for your phone. Considering that the Sony WH-1000XM4C launched in September, getting them for 34% off is a particularly attractive Black Friday deal . With premium sound, convenient controls, and features that make everyday listening more enjoyable, these headphones offer plenty of value at $198. passages: That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently.

extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. sources.title: OpenAI merges ChatGPT's Chat and Work modes, warns heavy users may hit limits sooner
passages: OpenAI has started rolling out a combined Chat and Work experience inside ChatGPT, putting two tools that used to be separate into one place.The update is currently reaching a small group of ChatGPT Pro subscribers.

According to OpenAI’s support page, the company plans to bring these shared usage limits to more users in December.What is actually changing?Until now, ChatGPT kept casual chats and heavy tasks in two different boxes.

You used Chat for everyday questions, writing, and quick help, while Work handled bigger jobs involving files, plugins, research, and connected apps.By putting them under one roof, OpenAI wants to make the chatbot easier to use.

In its email to subscribers, the company said users will now be able to move straight from brainstorming an idea to getting it done, like building a website, creating a presentation, or running web tasks—without jumping between tabs.However, OpenAI clarified that Codex will remain a separate experience inside the ChatGPT desktop app.The catch is how your usage gets counted.
OpenAI also said it is working to make its systems more efficient so paying users can get more out of their plans.What happens if you run out of your limit?There is still a safety net for daily use.

As more people demand smarter and more powerful AI models, companies are dealing with rising infrastructure costs and heavy strain on their computing power, forcing them to keep a tighter check on their most demanding users.- EndsAlso Read | OpenAI calls GPT 6.2 Astra and Sol price drop a mistake, users hit back for not getting discountAlso Read | Ex-OpenAI researcher says Anthropic is hyperstitioning AI race, Sam Altman reactsAlso Read | Ex-OpenAI researcher says Anthropic insiders fear AI could kill us all, but feel forced to build it
As per OpenAI’s Help Center, how fast your limit drains depends on the AI model you pick and how heavy your task is.
Many heavy users feel that combining two separate limits into one shared pool is a downgrade.
OpenAI product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux confirmed the rollout in a post on X on Tuesday.
More advanced models and complex jobs will use up your quota faster.Speaking to TechCrunch, an OpenAI spokesperson said most people will not notice more frequent usage resets.
OpenAI has confirmed that chats using the Instant model will remain unlimited and will not count toward your shared quota.
This comes right after OpenAI emailed subscribers to let them know the merger was on the way.

OpenAI has started rolling out a combined Chat and Work experience inside ChatGPT, putting two tools that used to be separate into one place.The update is currently reaching a small group of ChatGPT Pro subscribers. OpenAI product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux confirmed the rollout in a post on X on Tuesday. This comes right after OpenAI emailed subscribers to let them know the merger was on the way. According to OpenAI’s support page, the company plans to bring these shared usage limits to more users in December.What is actually changing?Until now, ChatGPT kept casual chats and heavy tasks in two different boxes. You used Chat for everyday questions, writing, and quick help, while Work handled bigger jobs involving files, plugins, research, and connected apps.By putting them under one roof, OpenAI wants to make the chatbot easier to use. In its email to subscribers, the company said users will now be able to move straight from brainstorming an idea to getting it done, like building a website, creating a presentation, or running web tasks—without jumping between tabs.However, OpenAI clarified that Codex will remain a separate experience inside the ChatGPT desktop app.The catch is how your usage gets counted. As per OpenAI’s Help Center, how fast your limit drains depends on the AI model you pick and how heavy your task is. OpenAI also said it is working to make its systems more efficient so paying users can get more out of their plans.What happens if you run out of your limit?There is still a safety net for daily use. relevantPassages.text: OpenAI has started rolling out a combined Chat and Work experience inside ChatGPT, putting two tools that used to be separate into one place.The update is currently reaching a small group of ChatGPT Pro subscribers.

According to OpenAI’s support page, the company plans to bring these shared usage limits to more users in December.What is actually changing?Until now, ChatGPT kept casual chats and heavy tasks in two different boxes.

You used Chat for everyday questions, writing, and quick help, while Work handled bigger jobs involving files, plugins, research, and connected apps.By putting them under one roof, OpenAI wants to make the chatbot easier to use.

In its email to subscribers, the company said users will now be able to move straight from brainstorming an idea to getting it done, like building a website, creating a presentation, or running web tasks—without jumping between tabs.However, OpenAI clarified that Codex will remain a separate experience inside the ChatGPT desktop app.The catch is how your usage gets counted.
OpenAI also said it is working to make its systems more efficient so paying users can get more out of their plans.What happens if you run out of your limit?There is still a safety net for daily use.

As more people demand smarter and more powerful AI models, companies are dealing with rising infrastructure costs and heavy strain on their computing power, forcing them to keep a tighter check on their most demanding users.- EndsAlso Read | OpenAI calls GPT 6.2 Astra and Sol price drop a mistake, users hit back for not getting discountAlso Read | Ex-OpenAI researcher says Anthropic is hyperstitioning AI race, Sam Altman reactsAlso Read | Ex-OpenAI researcher says Anthropic insiders fear AI could kill us all, but feel forced to build it
As per OpenAI’s Help Center, how fast your limit drains depends on the AI model you pick and how heavy your task is.
Many heavy users feel that combining two separate limits into one shared pool is a downgrade.
OpenAI product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux confirmed the rollout in a post on X on Tuesday.
More advanced models and complex jobs will use up your quota faster.Speaking to TechCrunch, an OpenAI spokesperson said most people will not notice more frequent usage resets.
OpenAI has confirmed that chats using the Instant model will remain unlimited and will not count toward your shared quota.
This comes right after OpenAI emailed subscribers to let them know the merger was on the way.

extraction.body: OpenAI has begun rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT for select users across the world. The move comes despite some subscribers voicing concerns that the merger could limit their usage. The company's product lead, Thibault Tibo Sottiaux, announced the rollout in a post on social media platform X. The latest update merges ChatGPT's conversational and work-focused features into a single interface. It also introduces a shared cap on data usage across both services. This change has some users worried that they could hit their limits faster if they rely heavily on advanced AI models. However, OpenAI has clarified that most users shouldn't see more frequent resets with this new system. Despite the changes, OpenAI's Instant model will continue to offer unlimited access. Conversations using this model won't count toward the shared usage cap. Even after reaching their combined limits, users can keep using Instant. An OpenAI spokesperson said they are working on making systems more efficient so subscribers can get more out of their plans. The changes have sparked debate among users, with some worried about having less access to advanced reasoning models due to the merger of Chat and Work allowances. There are also discussions about the lack of added value with the same subscription fees and losing flexibility with combined usage limits. OpenAI plans to roll out the unified system more widely in December, according to its support page.

extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. While Bitcoin (BTC) may not be as attractive a speculation with prices remaining flat, Bloomberg Intelligence Senior ETF analyst Eric Balchunas believes the most loyal holders of the cryptocurrency are not going anywhere anytime soon. Some of the Bitcoin investors are "tourists", he said, but the "true believers" are still buying in the $50,000 to $60,000s range, betting that governments' inability to increase the supply of Bitcoin will pay off in the long run. People pile into anything that's moving, Brown said. When Bitcoin is stagnant for a long time, he said, they chase something else. Balchunas agreed with it but only partly. "I agree. There's a tourist element to Bitcoin holders, but there's also the true believers," he said. Those believers seem convinced at around $50,000 to $60,000, Balchunas added as their faith is based on the debasement trade. "I just think there does have to be a more fundamental story for the people to actually make a $60,000 base. Those people believe what I'm just telling you about money printing in the gut," said the Senior ETF analyst. When host Batnick asked what they thought the next move in crypto would look like, Balchunas said more money printing. He referred to the COVID time and how the government threw 4 trillion at the problem, which edged the cryptocurrency market higher. Batnick didn't buy it. He said that Bitcoin's price only gets higher when people see others are buying the asset. In his view, "price itself is the catalyst." I might need to rise back to $80,000 to get people to buy again, Batnick said. Brown pointed out that legal sports betting has become a bigger problem for crypto because it competes for the same gambling money. He said he is in it "for the use cases, of which there are still none." Balchunas took issue with the notion that crypto is all guesswork. He said 50 million people own Bitcoin in the U.S. The network had been operating bossless for 17 years, which was "a minor miracle". Two years ago he would have agreed, said Balchunas. "I think ETFs cleaned up the industry," he said. It has become an asset class since the introduction of exchange-traded funds, he said. Seyffart added that anything that goes up thousands of percent is going to attract the worst people, like every bubble. That's especially true, he said, when people throw coins with nothing behind them. Bitcoin's price was trading at $59,811, down over 3% in the last 24 hours. Balchunas joined his fellow colleague and Bloomberg analyst James Seyffart in a podcast with Ritholtz Wealth Management's Michael Batnick and Josh Brown on Wednesday where they were asked a series of questions regarding the cryptocurrency market.

People pile into anything that's moving, Brown said. When Bitcoin is stagnant for a long time, he said, they chase something else. Balchunas agreed with it but only partly. "I agree. There's a tourist element to Bitcoin holders, but there's also the true believers," he said.

Those believers seem convinced at around $50,000 to $60,000, Balchunas added as their faith is based on the debasement trade. "I just think there does have to be a more fundamental story for the people to actually make a $60,000 base. Those people believe what I'm just telling you about money printing in the gut," said the Senior ETF analyst.

When host Batnick asked what they thought the next move in crypto would look like, Balchunas said more money printing. He referred to the COVID time and how the government threw 4 trillion at the problem, which edged the cryptocurrency market higher.

Batnick didn't buy it. He said that Bitcoin's price only gets higher when people see others are buying the asset. In his view, "price itself is the catalyst." I might need to rise back to $80,000 to get people to buy again, Batnick said. Brown pointed out that legal sports betting has become a bigger problem for crypto because it competes for the same gambling money. He said he is in it "for the use cases, of which there are still none."
Balchunas took issue with the notion that crypto is all guesswork. He said 50 million people own Bitcoin in the U.S. The network had been operating bossless for 17 years, which was "a minor miracle".
Two years ago he would have agreed, said Balchunas. "I think ETFs cleaned up the industry," he said. It has become an asset class since the introduction of exchange-traded funds, he said.

Seyffart added that anything that goes up thousands of percent is going to attract the worst people, like every bubble. That's especially true, he said, when people throw coins with nothing behind them.

extraction.body: SOMATOM go.Sim and SOMATOM go.Open Pro help customers meet challenges in RT treatment planning December 12, 2019 — The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared the SOMATOM go.Sim and SOMATOM go.Open Pro – two computed tomography (CT) systems from Siemens Healthineers that are dedicated for radiation therapy (RT) planning. The 64-slice SOMATOM go.Sim and 128-slice SOMATOM go.Open Pro are members of the SOMATOM go. platform , which was created to limit potential errors in radiation therapy planning and reduce time to treatment. The platform integrates hardware and software components such as patient marking lasers and automated quality assurance to simplify the treatment planning process, while the 85 cm bore accommodates positioning accessories and improves patient comfort. An innovative mobile workflow walks the radiation therapist through the setup process while the therapist remains with the patient to reduce anxiety. Since 75 percent of respiratory patients breathe irregularly, motion artifacts often appear in 4D image sets. The Direct Intelligent 4D (Direct i4D) technology of the SOMATOM go.Open Pro adapts image acquisition to patient breathing in real time to reduce those artifacts. Reducing unwarranted variations in the images can potentially decrease target margins, thereby sparing healthy tissue. “With the FDA clearance of the SOMATOM go.Sim and SOMATOM go.Open Pro, Siemens Healthineers offers our customers revolutionary technology for radiation therapy planning,” said Hanno Dotzel , vice president of surgery and cancer therapy in the Advanced Therapies business at Siemens Healthineers North America. “The new i4D technology can help our customers dramatically reduce image artifacts, enabling them to reach a new level of precision in radiation therapy treatment planning.” For more information: www.siemens-healthineers.us/rt-go-platform Siemens Healthineers Debuts Two CT Systems for Dedicated Radiotherapy Planning Oct. 23, 2026 — Coreline Soft has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for AVIEW Aorta ... The 64-slice SOMATOM go.Sim and 128-slice SOMATOM go.Open Pro are members of the SOMATOM go. platform , which was created to limit potential errors in radiation therapy planning and reduce time to treatment. The platform integrates hardware and software components such as patient marking lasers and automated quality assurance to simplify the treatment planning process, while the 85 cm bore accommodates positioning accessories and improves patient comfort. An innovative mobile workflow walks the radiation therapist through the setup process while the therapist remains with the patient to reduce anxiety.

Since 75 percent of respiratory patients breathe irregularly, motion artifacts often appear in 4D image sets. The Direct Intelligent 4D (Direct i4D) technology of the SOMATOM go.Open Pro adapts image acquisition to patient breathing in real time to reduce those artifacts. Reducing unwarranted variations in the images can potentially decrease target margins, thereby sparing healthy tissue.

“With the FDA clearance of the SOMATOM go.Sim and SOMATOM go.Open Pro, Siemens Healthineers offers our customers revolutionary technology for radiation therapy planning,” said Hanno Dotzel , vice president of surgery and cancer therapy in the Advanced Therapies business at Siemens Healthineers North America. “The new i4D technology can help our customers dramatically reduce image artifacts, enabling them to reach a new level of precision in radiation therapy treatment planning.”
For more information: www.siemens-healthineers.us/rt-go-platform

sources.body: PVmed, the developer of PV-iCurve Pro, said the software improves efficiency in radiation therapy planning with preset templates that provide image contouring immediately upon image receipt and forwards results to treatment planning systems.

extraction.body: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted 510(k) clearance for the PV-iCurve Pro software, which provides automated contouring of computed tomography (CT) images for radiation oncologists. PVmed, the developer of PV-iCurve Pro, said the software improves efficiency in radiation therapy planning with preset templates that provide image contouring immediately upon image receipt and forwards results to treatment planning systems. PV-iCurve Pro offers automated contouring of over 200 structures on CT, according to PVmed. The company said these structures include organs at risk as well as lymph node regions across the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis. With multiple editing tools (including thresholding, margin expansion and a Boolean structure calculator) and browser-based deployment, PVmed said the PV-iCurve Pro software enables clinician review and editing of contours from any terminal in the hospital.

sources.body: PVmed, the developer of PV-iCurve Pro, said the software improves efficiency in radiation therapy planning with preset templates that provide image contouring immediately upon image receipt and forwards results to treatment planning systems.

extraction.body: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted 510(k) clearance for the PV-iCurve Pro software, which provides automated contouring of computed tomography (CT) images for radiation oncologists. PVmed, the developer of PV-iCurve Pro, said the software improves efficiency in radiation therapy planning with preset templates that provide image contouring immediately upon image receipt and forwards results to treatment planning systems. PV-iCurve Pro offers automated contouring of over 200 structures on CT, according to PVmed. The company said these structures include organs at risk as well as lymph node regions across the head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis. With multiple editing tools (including thresholding, margin expansion and a Boolean structure calculator) and browser-based deployment, PVmed said the PV-iCurve Pro software enables clinician review and editing of contours from any terminal in the hospital.

extraction.body: NEW YORK (WABC) -- New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's have decided to postpone the annual Thanksgiving Day parade. Macy's released a statement that said, "With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed." The parade will now step off on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. This is the first time the parade has been postponed because of weather. It was canceled from 1942 to 1944 during World War II. The approaching storm threatened to ground the balloons and drench spectators. The National Weather Service had already issued a high wind warning before the call was made to move the parade. The most significant weather-related disruption before this year came in 1971, when high winds grounded all giant balloons. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic led to a scaled-back celebration without spectators. The balloons were deflated Wednesday night, and in a 6 p.m. news conference, Macy's Executive Producer Will Coss confirmed that there will not be a second inflation celebration Friday night, but instead the balloons will be brought back to New Jersey to be prepped for the parade, and the reinflation Friday would not be open to the public. Coss said the balloons need to be prepared again in a significantly shortened timeframe. "They have to do back and the be parade readied again, which is a weeks-long process that is going to get condensed to about 24 hours," he said. Coss reiterated that Macy's is "heartbroken," but said safety is paramount. During the evening briefing, Mayor Zohram Mamdani said safety will "always be our top priority." He said the storm will come with widespread coastal flooding at high tide and wind gusts of 60 mph, well in excess of what is permissible for the balloons. He acknowledged the disappointment but promised a "truly spectacular " parade that is also safe. Unfortunately, Mamdani confirmed he will not be at the parade on Saturday because of his upcoming surgery. As for security, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there is no specific or credible threat, but the department will call in over 1,000 officers to work Saturday. "By moving the parade to Saturday when weather conditions are much more favorable, we can give New Yorkers the celebration that they've been looking forward to without compromising on safety," Tisch said. Tisch also said officers who were going to work Thursday on overtime can now spend the day with the family if they choose and more officers will be scheduled for Saturday. Meanwhile, spectators who had traveled from around the world were left dumbstruck when Eyewitness News reporter Joelle Garguilo broke the news to them Wednesday afternoon that the parade had been postponed. They were left scrambling to figure out whether they could extend their stay to catch the parade on Saturday. Among those disappointed by the postponement were the Welsh family from Kansas, who were visiting New York City for the first time and planned to return home Friday. "I'm very disappointed. We waited, I waited, to go to New York City until they were old enough to experience the parade," Melissa Welsh said. Another visitor said, "Very big bummer. My whole life I wanted to come to this. Our nephew is in the parade in a marching band."

Macy's released a statement that said, "With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed."
The parade will now step off on Saturday at 8:30 a.m.
This is the first time the parade has been postponed because of weather. It was canceled from 1942 to 1944 during World War II.
The approaching storm threatened to ground the balloons and drench spectators.
The National Weather Service had already issued a high wind warning before the call was made to move the parade.

The most significant weather-related disruption before this year came in 1971, when high winds grounded all giant balloons. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic led to a scaled-back celebration without spectators.

Meanwhile, spectators who had traveled from around the world were left dumbstruck when Eyewitness News reporter Joelle Garguilo broke the news to them Wednesday afternoon that the parade had been postponed. Among those disappointed by the postponement were the Welsh family from Kansas, who were visiting New York City for the first time and planned to return home Friday.

extraction.body: European defense technology company Stark has unveiled the Vanta 24, a 24-meter uncrewed surface vessel developed to counter asymmetric threats in the Baltic Sea region, at the Bloomberg Tech event in London. European defense technology company Stark has announced the design of the Vanta 24 uncrewed surface vessel (USV). The vessel has been developed to provide a maritime security capability against asymmetric threats in the Baltic Sea region. The design was first shown in early November at the Bloomberg Tech event in London. Stark is continuing development work on the 24-meter vessel. According to the company's press release, the vessel will be built at shipyards in the United Kingdom and elsewhere in Europe. The modular design will support serial production; Stark says this production capacity will contribute to deterrence and the needs of contemporary warfare. The Vanta 24 will operate with an AI-enabled command and control system. The company said the vessel can operate alongside crewed platforms of the UK Royal Navy and other NATO navies, or independently. Beyond the Baltic, the aim is to establish a persistent presence in the North Atlantic and the High North as well. According to Stark, the vessel will answer NATO navies' need for cost-effective and scalable systems. The Baltic Sea became a focus of NATO surveillance activity after incidents between October 2023 and January 2026 in which cables and pipelines forming critical undersea infrastructure on the seabed were damaged. NATO officials linked these incidents to commercial vessels dragging their anchors along the seabed. "Shadow fleet" vessels, assessed as helping Russia circumvent sanctions on its oil exports, are also active in the region. As NATO navies stepped up surveillance of these ships, the Russian Federation Navy also assigned surface units to escort them. According to Stark, the Vanta 24 is designed to escort naval surface vessels, protect critical undersea infrastructure sites and monitor shadow fleet movements. Its capabilities will include long-range radar, anti-ship missiles and a 30 mm gun. The vessel is stated to have a 50-ton payload capacity and a speed capability of more than 35 knots. It will be able to remain at sea for several weeks, even in rougher sea conditions. The Vanta 24 is the largest member of the family, following the Vanta 6 and Vanta 12. The Vanta 6 emerged in late 2025, while the Vanta 12 was introduced in September 2026 at REPMUS, the Portuguese Navy and NATO experimentation activity held off southern Portugal. All three vessels operate with Stark's AI-based Minerva command and control software. The software is integrated into both the vessels and the ground control station where operators plan, task and monitor missions. Minerva can also connect to the command and control networks of NATO allies. According to Stark, the six-meter Vanta 6 focused on surveillance and port defense and carried a loitering munition within a total payload of 750 kilograms. The 12-meter Vanta 12 expanded surveillance and strike range with the addition of MBDA's Sea Venom anti-ship missile within its two-ton payload. Stark said the Vanta 24 is currently going through tooling and production processes at facilities in Germany and the United Kingdom, with initial demonstration phases planned for 2027. As incidents involving critical undersea infrastructure continued, NATO launched the Baltic Sentry enhanced surveillance activity in January 2025. The activity builds on the Alliance's standing naval groups focused on the North Atlantic. In the same month, the Task Force X experimentation structure was also set up, aiming to rapidly field advanced technologies, particularly uncrewed systems. Under Task Force X Baltic, NATO built up and tested a USV presence in the region throughout 2025 with commercial USV suppliers. In mid-2025, simultaneous maritime activities involving more than 70 USVs were carried out in the Baltic. According to commentary from Naval News, the Vanta 24's range, endurance and capability could provide a persistent presence in patrol, escort and infrastructure security tasks while operating independently. passages: Home » Stark Unveils Vanta 24 USV to Bolster Baltic Undersea Security

European defence technology company Stark has unveiled its Vanta 24 uncrewed surface vessel (USV) design. The USV has been conceived specifically to provide maritime security capability for countering asymmetric threats in the Baltic Sea region.

Currently, Stark is continuing to develop the 24-metre vessel – which was revealed at the Bloomberg Tech event in London in early November. In a press statement, the company highlighted: the intent to build the USV in shipyards in the UK and elsewhere in Europe; the use of a modular design to support mass production, with such mass underpinning capacity to generate deterrence and meet other contemporary warfare requirements; and the vessel being operated using artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced command and control (C2).
The company added that Vanta 24 is designed to deploy alongside UK Royal Navy (RN) and other NATO navy crewed platforms, or to operate independently.

Alongside the Baltic, Vanta 24 is designed to generate sustained presence across North Atlantic waters and up into the High North too, including in the varying environmental and operational conditions found across those regions.

In these operational contexts, Stark continued, Vanta 24 was conceived to support NATO navies’ needs to introduce affordable, scalable systems that can help generate persistent patrol, detection, tracking, and strike capabilities, as part of ‘hybrid’, crewed/uncrewed force structures and operational concepts.
“Vanta 24 will give [a] ‘hybrid navy’ a heavyweight combatant built for the Baltic,” Johannes Schaback, Stark’s Chief Technology Officer, said in the statement.

The Baltic Sea has become a focus for NATO maritime security surveillance and tracking activities, following several incidents between October 2023 and January 2026 in which critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) cables and pipelines on the seabed were damaged. NATO officials attributed these incidents to rogue commercial ships deliberately dragging their anchors across those CUI links.

The Baltic has also seen significant activity involving ‘shadow fleet’ ships – vessels perceived to be supporting Russian efforts to circumvent oil export sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. NATO navies’ consequent growing emphasis on surveilling the ‘shadow fleet’ has seen the Russian Federation Navy in turn deploy surface vessels to escort such shipping.

Reflecting the capability and operational requirements of these asymmetric challenges, Stark said Vanta 24 is designed to escort naval surface ships, guard CUI nodes, and monitor ‘shadow fleet’ movements. Its capabilities, Stark added, are set to include long-range radar, anti-ship missiles (ASMs), and a 30 mm gun. Platform statistics encompass a 50-tonne payload capacity, a sprint speed greater than 35 kt, and capacity to stay at sea for multiple weeks including in heavier sea states.
In its statement, Stark set out details of the Vanta family.

Vanta 24 follows the Vanta 6 and Vanta 12 USVs, and is the largest of the three. Vanta 6 emerged in late 2025, and Vanta 12 was launched at the Portuguese Navy/NATO ‘REPMUS’ operational experimentation (OPEX) activity in southern Portugal in September 2026.

All three Vantas operate using the company’s AI-based Minerva C2 software, which is integrated both onboard the USVs and in a ground control station (where operators plan, task, and supervise missions). Minerva can be connected across NATO allies’ C2 networks, too.

From the six-metre Vanta 6, to the 12-metre Vanta 12, to the 24-metre Vanta 24, the USV family’s evolution through ever-larger sizes brings the addition of greater range and endurance, plus enabling embarkation of different capabilities. Stark’s statement noted that Vanta 6 focused on surveillance and harbour defence, and carried a loitering munition, within a 750 kg total payload; Vanta 12 brought extended surveillance and strike range, the latter including the addition of MBDA’s Sea Venom ASM, within the USV’s two-tonne payload.
Stark said Vanta 24 currently is going through tooling and production processes at facilities in Germany and the UK, with initial demonstration milestones set for 2027.
USVs have been central within NATO’s response to the Baltic’s asymmetric maritime threats.

Amid the CUI incidents, in January 2025 NATO established the ‘Baltic Sentry’ enhanced vigilance activity, based around its North Atlantic-focused standing naval forces (SNFs) and designed to build presence, surveillance, and deterrence against the rogue threats.

Also in January 2025, NATO established the Task Force X OPEX construct, designed to rapidly harness enhanced technology – particularly uncrewed systems – to counter such threats at sea. The first iteration was Task Force X – Baltic; across 2025, NATO worked with commercial USV suppliers to build and test USV presence across the region.

The ‘Baltic Sentry’ and Task Force X – Baltic workstrands were also tied together on several occasions, with USVs working with surface ships from the SNFs to build integrated crewed/uncrewed – ie., hybrid – presence and mass in the region. In mid-2025, for example, parallel at-sea activities were conducted across the Baltic involving over 70 USVs.

When working with the SNFs to counter threats including the CUI risk, the USVs’ role was to provide visible presence and speed of response. Should a rogue commercial vessel appear to be loitering near a CUI site, a USV could deploy at speed to help provide deterrence presence, plus identification to assist with attribution.

In operational terms, Vanta 24’s range, endurance, mass, and capability would enable it to provide persistent presence when operating independently, conducting patrol, escort, or CUI security taskings and freeing up ‘exquisite’ platforms like destroyers and frigates to focus on the higher-end taskings their outputs are optimised for. When deploying with a task group, Vanta 24 can provide forward-deployed screening of the high-value crewed assets, pushing sensing and strike range out ahead at distance.

In a press statement, the company highlighted: the intent to build the USV in shipyards in the UK and elsewhere in Europe; the use of a modular design to support mass production, with such mass underpinning capacity to generate deterrence and meet other contemporary warfare requirements; and the vessel being operated using artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced command and control (C2).
The company added that Vanta 24 is designed to deploy alongside UK Royal Navy (RN) and other NATO navy crewed platforms, or to operate independently.

Alongside the Baltic, Vanta 24 is designed to generate sustained presence across North Atlantic waters and up into the High North too, including in the varying environmental and operational conditions found across those regions.

In these operational contexts, Stark continued, Vanta 24 was conceived to support NATO navies’ needs to introduce affordable, scalable systems that can help generate persistent patrol, detection, tracking, and strike capabilities, as part of ‘hybrid’, crewed/uncrewed force structures and operational concepts.

NATO officials attributed these incidents to rogue commercial ships deliberately dragging their anchors across those CUI links.

NATO navies’ consequent growing emphasis on surveilling the ‘shadow fleet’ has seen the Russian Federation Navy in turn deploy surface vessels to escort such shipping.

Reflecting the capability and operational requirements of these asymmetric challenges, Stark said Vanta 24 is designed to escort naval surface ships, guard CUI nodes, and monitor ‘shadow fleet’ movements. Its capabilities, Stark added, are set to include long-range radar, anti-ship missiles (ASMs), and a 30 mm gun. Platform statistics encompass a 50-tonne payload capacity, a sprint speed greater than 35 kt, and capacity to stay at sea for multiple weeks including in heavier sea states.
In its statement, Stark set out details of the Vanta family.

Vanta 24 follows the Vanta 6 and Vanta 12 USVs, and is the largest of the three. Vanta 6 emerged in late 2025, and Vanta 12 was launched at the Portuguese Navy/NATO ‘REPMUS’ operational experimentation (OPEX) activity in southern Portugal in September 2026.

All three Vantas operate using the company’s AI-based Minerva C2 software, which is integrated both onboard the USVs and in a ground control station (where operators plan, task, and supervise missions). Minerva can be connected across NATO allies’ C2 networks, too.

From the six-metre Vanta 6, to the 12-metre Vanta 12, to the 24-metre Vanta 24, the USV family’s evolution through ever-larger sizes brings the addition of greater range and endurance, plus enabling embarkation of different capabilities. Stark’s statement noted that Vanta 6 focused on surveillance and harbour defence, and carried a loitering munition, within a 750 kg total payload; Vanta 12 brought extended surveillance and strike range, the latter including the addition of MBDA’s Sea Venom ASM, within the USV’s two-tonne payload.

Also in January 2025, NATO established the Task Force X OPEX construct, designed to rapidly harness enhanced technology – particularly uncrewed systems – to counter such threats at sea. The first iteration was Task Force X – Baltic; across 2025, NATO worked with commercial USV suppliers to build and test USV presence across the region.

The ‘Baltic Sentry’ and Task Force X – Baltic workstrands were also tied together on several occasions, with USVs working with surface ships from the SNFs to build integrated crewed/uncrewed – ie., hybrid – presence and mass in the region. In mid-2025, for example, parallel at-sea activities were conducted across the Baltic involving over 70 USVs.

extraction.body: Bloomberg traced the lineage of one GB300 server rack to Gigabyte Technology. Well, this is awkward. Bloomberg reports it may have found evidence of a link between a Chinese data center with NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang's brief resignation from the company . Looking through documents two different firms submitted to Chinese regulators, the outlet found mention of GB300 NVL72 and GB200 server racks at the Yangtze River Delta Project in Shanghai. One of the companies, Shanghai Shuoyao, listed a GB300 NVL72 rack as collateral to secure an approximately $14 million loan from the Shanghai Innovation Bank. A single GB300 NVL72 unit houses 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 NVIDIA Grace processors, and can weigh about 3,300 pounds. US export rules require a license to ship these Blackwell systems to China. As Bloomberg notes, Jensen Huang once claimed GB300 racks are too big to smuggle. It's unclear how the GB300 and GB200 units made their way to the Shanghai facility, which may eventually house as many as 800,000 servers. However, Bloomberg was able to partly track the lineage of the GB300 unit. By putting the serial of the rack into a public warranty database, the outlet was able to trace it back to Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology, which PC gamers will know as one of NVIDIA's many add-in board partners. Like other NVIDIA AIBs, Gigabyte buys GPU chips from the company that it then uses to manufacture graphics cards for consumers and servers for enterprise customers. Gigabyte declined to answer Bloomberg's questions about what company or party originally bought the GB300 rack. A spokesperson told the outlet it "conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," adding, "all transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time." Shanghai Shuoyao, the company that offered a GB300 as collateral, has ties with Megaspeed. Alice Huang took a controlling stake in the Singaporean cloud computing company in 2023 before leaving it in August 2025. Earlier this month, Shanghai Shuoyao said it was one of Megaspeed's service providers, but described its relationship with the company as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." According to Bloomberg , Megaspeed used renderings of the Yangtze River Delta Project in a presentation it shared with investors in 2024. The deck did not list China as the location of the data center. Bloomberg notes it does not have evidence that Megaspeed directly diverted NVIDIA chips to the data center, and the company denies any wrongdoing . The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules . NVIDIA did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request. Alice Huang appears to have had a number of other ties to the Yangtze River Delta Project. Most notably, through Kang Wei, the man The New York Times reports was often introduced as her husband and appears to have had ties with China's Ministry of State Security. Bloomberg found him listed as the president of the facility. The publication also found evidence of servers containing NVIDIA's earlier Hopper-generation chips inside the Yangtze River Delta Project. Those GPUs are also illegal to ship to China without permission from the US government. Jensen Huang is set to testify publicly before Congress on December 3 at 10AM ET.
