extraction.body: Robinhood stock has been under pressure in the past few months and is now in the longest losing streak since it went public. HOOD has dropped in the last ten consecutive weeks and is hovering at its lowest level since April last year. This sell-off will likely gain momentum in the coming weeks as the crypto winter continues. HOOD stock has dropped sharply as the crypto winter gains momentum. Bitcoin ‘s price has dropped below $60,000, and most altcoins have had a steeper crash. For example, the World Liberty Financial (WLFI) token has crashed to a record low. Other top tokens like Cardano , Solana , and BNB Coin have continued falling. The valuation of all tokens has slumped sharply in this period and now stands at $2 trillion. All altcoins, including stablecoins, stand at less than $900 billion. The ongoing crypto market crash is happening because of the rising fear among investors. Indeed, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index has dropped to the extreme fear zone of 10. Investors are fearful because of the rising odds that the Federal Reserve will continue hiking interest rates in December. There are also concerns about the upcoming composition of the next Congress, in which Democrats will have the largest share. This composition means there will be substantial congressional investigations into the industry. The ongoing crypto winter will affect Robinhood. In its recent earnings report, Robinhood said that its crypto business continued to deteriorate in the last quarter. The company’s total revenue rose by 12% in the third quarter to over $1.42 billion. Its cryptocurrency revenue tumbled by 55% to $120 million. Another reason Robinhood stock is falling amid the ongoing crypto winter is because of its Robinhood Chain product. Data shows that the chain is losing momentum. The total value locked (TVL) in the network has dropped to $998 million from the year-to-date high of over $1 billion. The amount of stablecoins in the network has continued to fall, down from a high of $1.08 billion in September to $983 million today. Robinhood Chain’s DEX volume has also dropped in the past few months. It handled $16.4 billion this month, down from the September high of over $53.6 billion. This retreat has been driven by the ongoing crypto winter. In total, chain fees have been declining and currently stand at just $831,000 this month. At its peak, the network was making over $40.6 million. All these factors mean that Robinhood’s revenue growth will remain under pressure in the near term. Yahoo Finance data show that fourth-quarter revenue is expected to be $1.52 billion, up 18% from a year earlier. This growth was because of the ongoing diversification. The weekly chart shows that the Robinhood stock has been under pressure in the past few months. It has dropped over the last 10 consecutive weeks and is now trading at a crucial support level that coincides with its March low. This price also coincides with the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level. The stock has plunged below the 50-week moving average and is below the Strong, Pivot, Reversal level of Murrey Math Lines. Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling as sellers target the key support level of $50. A move above the $80 resistance level would invalidate the bearish outlook. Choosing between BigBear.ai ( BBAI +6.92% ) and Cerebras Systems ( CBRS +5.08% ) requires weighing government contracts against massive computing power.
These companies represent two distinct paths into the growing AI market, offering investors a choice between specialized software and high-performance hardware.
The company's proprietary semiconductor chip technology enables AI systems to operate at faster speeds than those offered by larger competitors.
This contributed to Cerebras gaining AI tech giants OpenAI, Microsoft, and Oracle as customers.
Moreover, the software company's reliance on federal contracts keeps it exposed to sudden shifts to its top-line growth.

Its stock's lower valuation reflects this vulnerability, and until BigBear.ai can expand outside government dependence, Cerebras' innovative chips provide a better path to a return on your investment despite its stock's higher valuation.

The company has also navigated operational hurdles, including a $76.7 million goodwill impairment in late 2026 and legal challenges related to historical accounting restatements.
Furthermore, it depends on third-party cloud infrastructure from providers like Microsoft ( MSFT +0.60% ) and Amazon ( AMZN +3.96% ) , to deliver its software.
Meanwhile, BigBear.ai saw sales sink in 2025 after the U.S. government performed budget cuts.
However, the fact that the federal government could cut funding to BigBear.ai last year suggests its technology is not critical.
BigBear.ai focuses on AI-powered decision intelligence software, positioning itself as a unique player among tech stocks serving the defense industry.
It uses a land and expand strategy by deploying minimally viable products to evaluate the potential for long-term government contracts.
Because it derives significant revenue from a limited number of defense and intelligence agencies, customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.
Cerebras Systems builds massive semiconductor infrastructure, including wafer-scale systems designed to train large-scale AI models more efficiently than traditional chips.
Its systems are used by organizations in medical research, cryptography, and energy, while its infrastructure is deployed in data centers worldwide.
This specialized focus helps the company target niche markets that require high-density computing power.

passages: Armstrong has adjusted his expectations before.
In 2025, he predicted Bitcoin would reach $1 million by 2030 but later revised that down to $300,000 to $400,000.
In September 2026, he reaffirmed his $400,000 target.
Bitcoin is trading around $59,200, which is 53.1% below its all-time high of $126,080.
For Bitcoin to hit $400,000, it needs a 576% increase, roughly 59.5% a year over the approximately 4.1 years left until the end of 2030.
Based on the current supply, that price would give Bitcoin a market cap of around $8 trillion, double the $4 trillion the entire crypto market first reached in 2025.
While Bitcoin surged about 7,961% over the past decade, it has gained only around 3.9% over the last five years, showing how long it can stall.
For exposure to Bitcoin without holding the coin directly, the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( NYSEARCA: BTC ) tracks spot Bitcoin, while Coinbase stock tends to swing even more.
The immediate challenge is whether Bitcoin can avoid falling further, as our look at whether Bitcoin drops below $50,000 weighs.

Bitcoin is trading around $59,200, which is 53.1% below its all-time high of $126,080. After a 22.7% drop in November, how realistic is it for Bitcoin to reach $400,000 by 2030?

For Bitcoin to hit $400,000, it needs a 576% increase, roughly 59.5% a year over the approximately 4.1 years left until the end of 2030. Based on the current supply, that price would give Bitcoin a market cap of around $8 trillion, double the $4 trillion the entire crypto market first reached in 2025.

Armstrong has adjusted his expectations before. In 2025, he predicted Bitcoin would reach $1 million by 2030 but later revised that down to $300,000 to $400,000. In September 2026, he reaffirmed his $400,000 target. His outlook hinges on Bitcoin’s four-year halving cycle, the planned reduction in how many new coins get created, and our look at whether Bitcoin can still reach $1 million by 2035 covers the longer-range case.

On November 27, Coinbase’s stock closed at $107, down 52.7% for the year, while Bitcoin is down 31.3%. Coinbase’s revenue decline is also notable, as third-quarter 2026 revenue fell 35% from a year earlier to $1.22 billion.

This gap is understandable, as Coinbase generates much of its revenue from trading fees. When cryptocurrency prices drop, trading activity tends to fall, so the company takes a hit from both lower prices and lower trading volume. Our December 2026 Bitcoin forecast covers where the coin could head next.

We think a $400,000 price for Bitcoin by 2030 looks unlikely. While Bitcoin surged about 7,961% over the past decade, it has gained only around 3.9% over the last five years, showing how long it can stall. A more realistic goal is for Bitcoin to climb back above its $126,080 all-time high by 2030, which would require a 113% increase from its current price.

extraction.body: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence could threaten the encryption systems protecting sensitive information worldwide, raising concerns among mathematicians and cybersecurity experts. In a report published Saturday, November 28, 2026, The Guardian cited credible indications that powerful AI models may have solved longstanding mathematical problems underlying digital security. Potential consequences include making it easier for malicious actors to access confidential communications, financial transactions, diplomatic correspondence and private emails.Governments, intelligence agencies, banks and technology companies could face pressure to replace vulnerable security systems much sooner than previously anticipated. The concerns follow several mathematical breakthroughs announced by major AI companies in recent weeks. According to The Guardian, these developments demonstrate that artificial intelligence may be capable of solving complex problems that researchers previously expected to remain unresolved for years.Cryptography underpins much of modern digital infrastructure. It protects electronic communications, financial payments and government information while also helping verify the identity of senders and ensuring that transmitted data has not been altered.Many established encryption methods depend on mathematical problems that computers can solve relatively easily in one direction but struggle to reverse without the correct cryptographic key. A significant breakthrough could therefore weaken protections used across international financial and communications networks. Scott Aaronson, a prominent theoretical computer scientist, wrote this week that information from several reliable sources had convinced him that AI laboratories were close to or had achieved major advances in cryptography. He described the developments as unprecedented for mathematics and computer science.Aaronson also emphasized that researchers must independently examine and verify mathematical proofs produced by AI companies. The reported discoveries have not yet established that existing encryption systems can be broken in practical conditions. He noted that the broader implications of recent mathematical discoveries, particularly their potential effects on encryption, remain uncertain.Du Sautoy also questioned the limited public discussion surrounding the mathematical foundations of electronic security. He suggested that uncertainty about whether fundamental problems had already been solved could explain why some researchers were reluctant to discuss the subject openly. Meanwhile, governments and technology companies have been preparing for another potential threat: quantum computing.Sufficiently advanced quantum computers could eventually break several established encryption algorithms, although experts have generally considered that possibility years away. Steven Murdoch, a computer science professor at University College London, said organizations were already developing and adopting encryption standards designed to withstand quantum computing attacks. However, implementation has progressed slowly.Murdoch identified approximately 2032 as a target for the transition to stronger encryption standards, adding that many organizations would probably struggle to meet even that deadline. Recent developments in artificial intelligence have increased concerns that cryptographic challenges could emerge much earlier.The precise nature of the potential AI discoveries remains unclear. According to The Guardian, researchers believe AI may have identified new methods for breaking encryption or, alternatively, demonstrated that certain mathematical shortcuts do not exist. Alan Woodward, a computer science professor at the University of Surrey, cautioned against assuming that a mathematical breakthrough would immediately make existing encryption systems ineffective.Applying theoretical discoveries to practical attacks would require overcoming additional technical obstacles. Woodward nevertheless warned that the speed of recent AI advances should encourage organizations to prepare for unexpected developments. Major banks and governments that depend on encryption could face serious difficulties if they cannot update their security infrastructure quickly enough.

passages: Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI.
In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.
While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications.
For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.
The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.
“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said.
“They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”
“The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued.
“We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing.
We’ll train both a small and a large model next year.
The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions.
Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”
Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said.
Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.
Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.
“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do.
“But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”
“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said.
“People often point to Palantir and other systems.
I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog.
But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications , on systems for detecting disinformation.
But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

extraction.body: Sakana AI , a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies. Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited. “When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.” Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version. The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks. “We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.” However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology. “The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.” While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises. “Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.” Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications , on systems for detecting disinformation. Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises. “Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said. While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources. Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month. But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public. The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself. “We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said. Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. passages: Sakana AI , a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.

Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.

“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”
Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.

The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.

“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”
However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.

“The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”

While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.

“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications , on systems for detecting disinformation.

Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.
“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.

While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.
Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.
But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.
“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said.

Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.

“We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha said. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”

passages: From apps that allow music playback without relying on a phone to clearing things off your to-do list, we've handpicked our favorite free Samsung Galaxy Watch apps available to download.
The new Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 even throw in a free 60-day Strava trial subscription.
With the Strava app on your Galaxy Watch, you're always a few taps away from your next outdoor run or biking trail.
Scenes are preset routines you can run to keep your mind off mundane tasks in your home, and they can also be triggered from a Galaxy Watch.
Unlike Fitbits, Samsung's Galaxy Watches let you download music onto your watch for offline playback if you've got a Spotify Premium subscription.
Having spent over eight years refining its Galaxy Watch lineup, Samsung has built a strong app ecosystem for its wearables that lets them do a whole lot more than fitness tracking.
The Wear OS app also offers watch complication features (strange name, I know) to create progress bars for daily and weekly goals or summaries of tasks left to complete today.

extraction.body: If you aren't using these, you're missing out. Having spent over eight years refining its Galaxy Watch lineup, Samsung has built a strong app ecosystem for its wearables that lets them do a whole lot more than fitness tracking. From apps that allow music playback without relying on a phone to clearing things off your to-do list, we've handpicked our favorite free Samsung Galaxy Watch apps available to download. We focused on non-Google apps, so this list won't have the likes of Google Keep's voice-to-text notes, YouTube Music or Google Wallet . We're big fans of Spotify's "daylist" and Discover Weekly playlists, and its Wear OS app lets you take them anywhere with the watch's onboard storage. If you're already on Strava, chances are you'd want your watch to log your next run. Todoist's simple interface lets you clear tasks and keep track of upcoming ones, while Citymapper is a boon for live transit users who track their commute. If you've got an array of smart home devices scattered around your home or workplace, SmartThings lets you control them all. Unlike Fitbits, Samsung's Galaxy Watches let you download music onto your watch for offline playback if you've got a Spotify Premium subscription. Leave the phone at home for your next run or gym workout now that you can bring your playlists with you. Spotify's massive catalog and mix of human curation and algorithm-powered playlists need no introduction, given it's the most popular music streaming platform around. While its free tier lacks offline downloads and badgers you with ads, it's still a great app to have on your smartwatch. Amazon Music and YouTube Music's Wear OS apps are great alternatives if you're already paying for a music streaming service subscription with one of them. Google Maps might be the de facto standard when it comes to navigation, but Citymapper's focus on urban transit in supported cities gives it better routing options for public transit. Live updates on trains and buses, including how many stops you have left, give it a leg up against Google's mapping service. The watch interface doesn't just show you the next train or bus. It shows you when subsequent vehicles arrive should you miss the first one to your destination. While you still need to take your phone out to type out places outside predefined Work and Home locations, it's a great app for your Galaxy Watch. Todoist keeps its interface simple, letting you add new tasks and subtasks or sort through your inbox of upcoming tasks. Voice-to-text support lets you dictate task information instead of typing it out on your watch. The day progress tile keeps you on track by showing you the number of daily tasks you've cleared. Reminders on larger projects can be set up on your smartphone, and they'll show up on your watch. The Wear OS app also offers watch complication features (strange name, I know) to create progress bars for daily and weekly goals or summaries of tasks left to complete today. If you've got a Samsung Galaxy Watch 4 or up, the SmartThings app lets your watch interact with a variety of devices. Adjust the volume or change channels on your TV, change up the mood at home with lighting controls and set the temperature on your air conditioner. You can also tweak speaker volume and get your robot vacuum cleaner to start cleaning or charging. While you need to add a new device via your phone, you can control these from your watch once you've set them up. Scenes are preset routines you can run to keep your mind off mundane tasks in your home, and they can also be triggered from a Galaxy Watch. It's a nifty way to automate your home, be it for a party trick or to optimize your routine. If you're looking for more workout insights than you find in the Samsung Health app, Strava has you covered. You can sync the two services together to share data like route information and the activities you've taken part in. The new Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 even throw in a free 60-day Strava trial subscription. With the Strava app on your Galaxy Watch, you're always a few taps away from your next outdoor run or biking trail. Depending on the activity, your watch will track and display metrics like heart rate, calories, distance or current speed even if you don't have your phone with you. You'll still need a smartphone to do things like put together a training plan.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia shifts Vision 2030 spending amid economic and security pressure - CNBC
passages: Saudi Arabia has been on a mammoth capital spending spree since it launched its Vision 2030 plan to reduce its dependence on oil revenue in 2016, deploying the resources of its sovereign wealth fund — the Public Investment Fund, or PIF.
Advisory group Oxford Economics forecasts a more negative outlook.

It sees the Saudi economy shrinking 3.4% this year and by 4% in 2027, amid escalating attacks on energy infrastructure even as a new minimum wage and continued Vision 2030 spending are expected to support incomes and domestic demand.
"Our forecasts already assume that some of the Vision 2030 targets will be achieved later than originally planned.
But the overarching goal of economic diversification remains unchanged," Samdani told CNBC by email.

Alibrahim also said Saudi Arabia would "stop at nothing from realizing long-term sustainable stability in the region" amid ongoing Houthi strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure that have killed and injured dozens and repeatedly rocked oil markets .

Neil Quilliam, managing director of consultancy Azure Strategy, said investors are assessing whether Houthi attacks demonstrate a persistent vulnerability that could increase the cost and complexity of delivering Vision 2030.

Saudi Arabia is meanwhile grappling with the destabilizing effects of ongoing strikes by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which have hit targets including the PIF tower , Riyadh Airport and the country's largest oil refinery .

"The phase we're in today is one where every riyal is deployed with greater precision... it was clear that while we want to diversify or restructure our economy to depend less on government spend, there was a lot of catch-up that needed to be done, and for that, you saw government spend leading the way," Alibrahim told CNBC's Dan Murphy.

"The government is managing fiscal pressures and shifting budgetary spending towards essential services and strategic priorities, while PIF is becoming more selective in its capital allocation and seeking greater private-sector participation," Samdani said, adding that some giga projects are being scaled back or delayed, while investment continues in sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, tourism, mining and technology.
"Right now, that is shifting from spending and delivery at any cost to spending and delivering at the right cost.

extraction.body: Saudi Arabia's economic diversification strategy has moved from "spending and delivery at any cost" to "spending and delivery at the right cost," Economy Minister Faisal Alibrahim told CNBC on Friday. It comes after the Kingdom scaled back or cut several flagship projects as it endures a sharp economic contraction. Alibrahim also said Saudi Arabia would "stop at nothing from realizing long-term sustainable stability in the region" amid ongoing Houthi strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure that have killed and injured dozens and repeatedly rocked oil markets . "The phase we're in today is one where every riyal is deployed with greater precision... it was clear that while we want to diversify or restructure our economy to depend less on government spend, there was a lot of catch-up that needed to be done, and for that, you saw government spend leading the way," Alibrahim told CNBC's Dan Murphy. "Right now, that is shifting from spending and delivery at any cost to spending and delivering at the right cost. We're moving towards a policy-first approach to many of our policy areas and... objectives. We're also creating a clearer business environment, one that aligns the regulatory environment in the Kingdom with international laws." That includes the recent announcement of a 15% minimum effective tax rate on multinational profits, which Alibrahim said would "create a clearer environment for the private sector to operate," as the government looks to attract more external investment. Saudi Arabia has been on a mammoth capital spending spree since it launched its Vision 2030 plan to reduce its dependence on oil revenue in 2016, deploying the resources of its sovereign wealth fund — the Public Investment Fund, or PIF. But more recently, it has reassessed the cost and commercial prospects of initiatives such as the new economic region NEOM and the futuristic "The Line" city , withdrawn funding from the LIV Golf tournament and halted construction on a planned giant skyscraper in Riyadh. In January, it said it would postpone hosting the 2029 Asian Winter Games, which had been scheduled for Trojena, a planned part of NEOM. Saudi Arabia is meanwhile grappling with the destabilizing effects of ongoing strikes by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which have hit targets including the PIF tower , Riyadh Airport and the country's largest oil refinery . The danger forced the Kingdom to call off its big international investor conference , dubbed "Davos in the Desert," which was due to be attended by some of the biggest figures in global finance in November. "The human cost of crisis has been real, and so has been the economic cost," Alibrahim told CNBC. Alibrahim said infrastructure investments had allowed the Kingdom's energy sector to restore production to near pre-crisis levels. It has meanwhile moved its import and export hub from the east to the west of the country via land-based transport due to the airport strikes, which has restored cargo levels. He added that the attacks highlight the importance of diversification to the Saudi economy. Real GDP contracted by 3.8% in the third quarter, according to government figures , with oil activities down 20.4% year-on-year partially offset by a 1.9% rise in non-oil activities. Net foreign direct investment inflows dropped 19.5% year-on-year in the second quarter. The Saudi Ministry of Finance expects an overall contraction of around 2.1% this year and a rebound of 10.9% next year. Advisory group Oxford Economics forecasts a more negative outlook. It sees the Saudi economy shrinking 3.4% this year and by 4% in 2027, amid escalating attacks on energy infrastructure even as a new minimum wage and continued Vision 2030 spending are expected to support incomes and domestic demand. Akanksha Samdani, lead economist at Oxford Economics, said Vision 2030 was entering a new phase focused on returns. "The government is managing fiscal pressures and shifting budgetary spending towards essential services and strategic priorities, while PIF is becoming more selective in its capital allocation and seeking greater private-sector participation," Samdani said, adding that some giga projects are being scaled back or delayed, while investment continues in sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, tourism, mining and technology. "Our forecasts already assume that some of the Vision 2030 targets will be achieved later than originally planned. But the overarching goal of economic diversification remains unchanged," Samdani told CNBC by email. Neil Quilliam, managing director of consultancy Azure Strategy, said investors are assessing whether Houthi attacks demonstrate a persistent vulnerability that could increase the cost and complexity of delivering Vision 2030. "They have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to target important economic infrastructure and expose weaknesses in Saudi air defences," he told CNBC, with the attacks challenging the "assumption that Saudi Arabia has insulated itself from regional instability." The economic impact of the strikes will be less about physical damage and more about whether they affect confidence in Saudi Arabia as a destination for tourism, entertainment and sports, a key part of Vision 2030 and a source of foreign capital and expatriate talent, he added.
